Chapter 14, the Yoga of the Threefold Division of the Guṇas (Guṇatrayavibhāgayoga), continues directly from chapter 13 with no question from Arjuna, as Kṛṣṇa promises to declare once more the supreme knowledge that has carried every sage before him to the highest perfection. He opens with a brief cosmogony — the great brahman as his womb, into which he places the seed from which every form in every realm arises — before turning to the chapter's central teaching: the three guṇas, sattva, rajas, and tamas, the constituent qualities of nature that bind the otherwise imperishable embodied self to the body. He defines each in turn: sattva as stainless and luminous, yet binding through attachment to happiness and to knowledge; rajas as passionate, born of craving, binding through attachment to action; tamas as born of ignorance, binding through heedlessness, laziness, and sleep. He describes how the three constantly contend for supremacy, the visible symptoms of each one's ascendancy, the destiny after death and the fruits of action and knowledge proper to each, and a ranked cosmology in which those who abide in sattva rise, those of rajas remain in the middle, and those of tamas sink down. True knowledge, he says, is to see that the guṇas alone act and to know what lies beyond them — the knowledge that frees the embodied soul from birth, death, old age, and suffering and grants immortality. Arjuna then asks how one who has gone beyond the three guṇas can be recognized, and Kṛṣṇa answers with a portrait of such a person: indifferent alike to the presence or absence of illumination, activity, and delusion; equal in pleasure and pain, in a clod of earth and gold, in blame and praise, in honor and dishonor, in friend and foe; and one who has given up every self-driven undertaking. He adds that whoever serves him with unwavering devotion crosses beyond the guṇas by that devotion alone and becomes fit for the state of being brahman. The chapter closes with Kṛṣṇa's declaration of himself as the very foundation of brahman — of the immortal and the imperishable, of the eternal dharma, and of unmixed happiness.
